title: The Colour of the Sand
logline: A cape of red ground at the end of a long park track, where a chronicle says somebody once put their hands on the earth, got up with copper-coloured palms, and accidentally named an entire country — and the ground is still lying there, the same colour, doing nothing at all.
human_question: If the oldest name for the whole country I live in is a description of the colour of a handful of dirt at one small cape, what is a name actually attached to?

place.what_kind_of_place: A low cape on an empty west-facing coast inside a national park: a cliff of deep red earth lying in courses over pale fossil-bearing limestone, running a couple of kilometres north from the point, with dry thorn scrub and wind-stunted trees behind it and open sea in front. There is no building, no shrine, no jetty and no settlement at the point itself. There is no monument of any kind, and nothing has been put up here to look at. What is on the ground instead is a surface: several hundred metres of it strewn with broken brick and an enormous quantity of broken pottery, the eroded remains of a trading town that is simply lying on top of the sand and being cut away by the sea. Reaching it means a long, slow drive on sand tracks inside a park whose gates open at six and close at six, in a licensed vehicle with a park tracker, and there is usually nobody else there.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off. The colour: a two-kilometre wall of red earth over white-grey limestone, facing an open sea, which at the end of the day takes the sun full in the face and goes the colour of a fired pot. The emptiness: a horizon with nothing on it at all, no vessel, no structure, no person, and heat haze thick enough that a long lens turns the far end of the cliff into three flat bands of colour with the air moving between them. And then the reversal of scale at the end, from that huge empty frame down to a close shot of dry red crumbs breaking between two fingers. It is a film with one landscape, no event and an intimate payoff, and it is the only piece in this group with no architecture and nobody in it.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, on purpose. The light swings round through the day and the cliff goes from flat brown at noon to saturated red in the last two hours. Heat haze thickens and thins. Wind off the sea moves the scrub constantly and moves nothing else; loose red dust lifts and drops. The sea is flat or it is not. A jeep track fills in behind the vehicle. Animals may cross at a distance and are filmed at a distance or not at all. Nothing in this film builds, arrives, is completed or is revealed; the change the film actually delivers is a change of lens.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry, bright part of the year, and the last two hours before the park closes, when the sun is out over the water and striking the red face directly. Because the gates open at six and shut at six and the point is a long way inside, there is no true sunrise or sunset available from the ground here: the film is made in hard daylight and late afternoon, and that is a discipline rather than a loss. Midday, usually the worst light anywhere, is the best light this film has for the long-lens haze work.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A hot, dry, almost silent landscape piece. A track through thorn scrub, a cape that opens onto an empty sea, a red cliff two kilometres long, air visibly moving over the ground, and then a ground so thick with broken pottery that it reads as a surface rather than as objects. It resolves on its own terms: arrive, look out, look down, leave. Nobody appears. Nothing happens. Its own beauty is the point and its payoff is the smallest shot in it.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the plainest demonstration in the series of a name and its basis being two separate things. The voice does not argue; it reports. The oldest recorded name for this entire country is, on the chronicle's own telling, a colour word taken from earth on somebody's hands at one cape — and that earth is in the frame, unchanged, unvisited, and no longer connected to anything the word now does. Then the camera looks down at a town that is now a scatter, and the voice gives the ordinary meaning of the word the texts use for a collection: a heap. Everything is here; the thing they were parts of is not; the only thing holding them together is somebody deciding to count them as one.

sequence.on_screen: Hard mid-morning. A long lens laid down the coast from the point: three flat bands — red ground, white rock, blue water — with heat visibly moving between them. The frame is held far longer than is comfortable. Nothing enters it.
sequence.voice: Nothing is going to happen here. This is a cape at the end of a track inside a national park, and there is no building on it, nothing to visit, and usually nobody here. The oldest written name anyone has for this whole country was, on one old account, invented on a beach like this one. It is not the name of a people, or a king, or a river. It is a word about a colour.

sequence.on_screen: Closer, from the beach looking up: the cliff face in raking light. Courses of deep red earth sitting on pale limestone full of fossil coral. Red dust running down the white rock in dry streaks.
sequence.voice: A chronicle compiled something like a thousand years after the event it describes says that men came ashore on this coast, sat down exhausted, put their hands on the ground to rest, and stood up with their palms stained the colour of copper. So they called the place after the colour on their hands, and a word meaning copper-coloured sand became the name of the district, and then of the whole island. The same tradition says they met people who were already living here. That part is not this film's business and nothing that follows needs it.

sequence.on_screen: From the clifftop, a very long lens out to sea. Empty horizon, doing nothing, for a long time. Then a slow pan along a shoreline with no mark of anybody on it.
sequence.voice: The chronicle is a chronicle. No excavation has ever confirmed the landing it describes, and which stretch of coast it means is argued about. But the word itself is not in doubt, because it travelled. An emperor on the far side of the strait had it carved into rock three centuries before the chronicle was written down. Greek geographers wrote it in their own spelling and Romans copied them, and a descendant of that spelling was still the name Europe used for this island fifteen hundred years later. The sound went out on ships. What it meant did not travel with it. That was supplied, each time, by whoever was listening.

sequence.on_screen: The smallest shot in the film. A hand, close, low, breaking a dry crumb of the red ground between finger and thumb; the dust on the skin; then the same red under the edge of a boot sole. No wider context in frame at all.
sequence.voice: This is the thing the name was a description of. It is still here. It is still that colour. Sixty-five thousand square kilometres now answer to a word for it. The colour is real — the texts are firm that a colour is one of the things that is actually there, not a word we agreed on. What the word got hung on afterwards is not a colour. It is a country, and a country is a name for a great many things at once.

sequence.on_screen: Inland twenty metres, off the cliff edge. A slow tilt down from the scrub line to the ground. The ground is broken pottery — hundreds of metres of it, thick, grey and red and black, mixed with broken brick, lying on sand. The camera moves along it and never touches it.
sequence.voice: Twenty metres back from the edge the ground changes. It is covered in broken pottery and broken brick, and it goes on like that for hundreds of metres. A port stood here. The first Roman ever to reach this island was blown off course and made landfall at a harbour on this coast in the reign of Claudius, and the Greeks already had a name for the harbour, made out of their own words for a horse and a mountain, because the local name meant horse mountain. The same meaning arrived; not one of the same sounds did. Pearls went out from here. A surveyor noticed the town in nineteen twenty-three, and the man who came after him put the pottery at no later than about fifty years before the Christian era.

sequence.on_screen: Static, high angle, a square metre of the surface filling the frame: rims, bases, curved wall fragments, brick, all of it in focus at once, none of it whole. Held. Then the identical framing pulled wide, so the same surface reads as one continuous texture to the scrub line.
sequence.voice: The word these texts use for a collection is the ordinary word for a heap. A heap of water. A heap of firewood. They sort its meanings and keep only that one: a heap, and a portion. Five heaps, they say, is everything there is — matter, feeling, recognising, forming, knowing — and each one is nothing but every item of its kind, past and future and present, near and far, coarse and fine, gathered in one place and given a single name. Look at this ground.

sequence.on_screen: A very slow track past the scatter at knee height, the sherds going out of focus one after another. Wind in the low scrub. Nobody. The light beginning to go orange.
sequence.voice: Every part of the town is here. The town is not. There is no basket, no wall, no floor plan, nothing on the site doing the gathering — and the collection still exists, because someone is standing here counting it as one thing. That is the whole operation the texts are describing, and they are not saying the town was never real or that you are not real. They are saying that the gathering happens in a mind, and that something which is only held together by being counted together can be put down.

sequence.on_screen: Last light on the cliff: the full two kilometres of red face taking the sun off the water, at the longest lens available, so the whole thing compresses into a single saturated band. No movement. The shot outlasts its welcome and then ends.
sequence.voice: Nothing here has been corrected. The name is not a mistake and nobody using it is wrong; the texts are careful about that, and they are just as careful to say that the everyday name of a place is the useful thing and not the enemy. The point is smaller and harder. A name and the thing it was taken from are two separate items. That word went out across the sea, came back unrecognisable, and is now the answer to a question about where you are from. And the ground it was a description of is lying here in the sun, the same colour it always was, with nobody to look at it.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the two digests meet on this ground rather than being bolted together. C084 supplies the machinery: paññatti is both the thing made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25], a name-concept is the name laid over the ultimates or over the eight kinds of concept [C084-P:L47], and the first of those kinds is the collective, whose listed examples are the earth, mountains, rivers and the sea [C084-P:L29]. The Mārgaya adds the two pieces this film actually films: the shape-concept, in which ground, mountain, tree and leaf are what the mind takes up from the configurations of the great elements [C084-M:L13], and the separation of sound from name, where the spoken sound is ultimately real and the name it carries is what arises in the hearer [C084-M:L21]. C077 supplies the plain word for what is left on the ground. The Pradeepika sorts the several senses of khandha and keeps only the heap sense, the one used when speaking of a great heap of water, expressly setting aside the conventional sense used of a great log of firewood, and states that the aggregates are characterised by heap-ness and by being portions [C077-P:L36–L42]; it shows the whole mass of one kind lumped together on all sides and displayed under one word [C077-P:L44], and gathers parts alike in a single characteristic into one place to make one heap [C077-P:L996–L998]; the Mārgaya says flatly that the word means collection [C077-M:L10]. Put on this cape, the two produce one argument twice over. A colour word taken from earth on somebody's hands became the name of sixty-five thousand square kilometres, and the earth is still there, unchanged and unconnected to anything the word now does. And a town that traded across an ocean is now a surface of sherds — every portion present, nothing left on site to gather them, and the collection surviving only because somebody is standing there counting it as one.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the sources' sixfold scheme of names has this exact case in it, and that the case is documentary rather than illustrative. The Mārgaya's own example of a name that takes something ultimately real as its basis and designates something not ultimately real is 'the white man': whiteness is a real state, it is colour-form; the man is not ultimately existent [C084-M:L29]. Change white to copper and you have the oldest recorded name of this country, precisely — a real colour, on a real cape, carrying a designation of a whole conventional whole. That is not a claim that the name is false; the digest is explicit that the existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories and not true and false, and the Pradeepika itself lists ground and mountain among the not-ultimately-existent and then records, without embarrassment, that people call them ground and mountain [C084-P:L55]. C077 then stops the film from settling into a piece about language. The word for a collection is the word for a heap, and the heap's reach is eleven-fold — past, future and present, internal and external, coarse and fine, inferior and superior, far and near [C077-P:L46–L57] — so the gathering plainly includes what is over and gone. The pairing also closes the film's two cheap endings. The scatter is not evidence that nothing is real: the same source says the division is there so that the grip of 'mine, a self' can be loosened [C077-P:L984; C077-M:L24] and elsewhere insists that suffering really exists and that it is only the separate owner of it that is missing [C077-P:L2292–L2298]. And the red earth is not a lesson about being one with the land; the source matches inside and outside element for element in order to show that neither side contains a self, which is the opposite of belonging.

concept_links.why: The digest's own definitions carry this film without stretching. Paññatti is both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25]; a name-concept is the name laid over either the ultimates or the eight kinds of concept [C084-P:L47]; and among the not-ultimately-existent the Pradeepika lists ground and mountain, then records that people call them ground and mountain [C084-P:L55]. The Mārgaya's shape-concept is the ground itself, taken up by the mind from the configurations of the great elements [C084-M:L13], and its division test is the one this site performs without help: divide a thing and if what seemed to be there disappears, it was a concept — cloth into thread [C084-M:L7]. The sharpest fit is the third of the six ways a name relates to its basis. The Mārgaya's example is 'the white man': white is a real state, it is colour-form, and the man is not ultimately existent, so the name takes something real as its basis and designates something that is not [C084-M:L29]. This cape gives that the largest referent anybody has ever attached to a colour. And the sound-versus-name distinction [C084-M:L21] is documentary here rather than asserted, because the same word physically travelled — carved in Prakrit on an emperor's rock, reshaped by Greek mouths, copied by Romans, and still in European use fifteen centuries later — with the meaning supplied fresh by each hearer, exactly as the text says. Every limit in the digest is load-bearing and is written into the beats. The film never tells anybody that the name they use is wrong: beat 8 says so outright, and beats 2 and 3 attribute the naming story to a chronicle rather than narrating it as event. The existent and non-existent pairs are never rendered as true and false. And 'language constructs reality' or 'nothing is real' is refused explicitly in beat 4, which says the colour is one of the things that actually is there.

C077 supplies the second ground and most of the guards. Khandha is glossed plainly as collection [C077-M:L10]; the Pradeepika keeps only the heap sense of the word, the sense used of a great heap of water, and expressly sets aside the conventional sense used of a great log of firewood, adding that the aggregates are characterised by heap-ness and by being portions [C077-P:L36–L42]; it then shows the whole mass of one kind lumped together on all sides under a single word [C077-P:L44] and forms one heap by gathering into one place the parts alike in a single characteristic [C077-P:L996–L998]. A surface of potsherds is that operation with the referent removed, and the eleven aspects across which the gathering runs — past, future, present, internal, external, coarse, fine, inferior, superior, far, near [C077-P:L46–L57] — are why a heap can include a town that stopped existing two thousand years ago. Four limits from the digest are written into the film rather than noted beside it. First, 'you do not exist' and 'the self is an illusion' are not what the source says: the division exists so that the firm grip of 'mine, a self' on each heap can be loosened [C077-P:L984; C077-M:L24], and the same text states that suffering really exists and only its separate owner is missing [C077-P:L2292–L2298]; beat 7 says this in as many words. Second, and specific to a film about red earth, the digest forbids the 'one with nature, made of stardust' reading: the source matches inside and outside element by element in order to show that neither side holds a self, not to offer a feeling of belonging, so nothing in this film suggests that the viewer is made of the same soil. Third, the taking-apart is not offered as a technique to try: where this source hands over a practice of dividing a thing it places it inside monastic discipline, under a teacher, with preconditions [C077-P:L1493–L1497], and the film gives nobody an exercise. Fourth, the inferior-and-superior ladder in the same range belongs to a cosmology of rebirth and a pre-modern social order [C077-P:L203–L207], so no era, no trade and no people in this film is graded against another — which also rules out any reading of the sherds as a fallen greatness.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a name and the thing a name was taken from are two separate items, and that the gap between them can be enormous without anybody having made a mistake. The proof needs no belief and no argument: a colour on the ground at one cape, and a word for that colour that now covers a country, with the colour still lying there in the sun. And the second half: that a collection can go on existing after the thing collected has gone, because the collecting was never on the ground in the first place.
what_must_be_real: The ground is filmed and nothing on it is handled. This is a declared archaeological site with no conservation presence and a documented history of visitors carrying material away, so no potsherd, brick, bone or worked stone is picked up, turned over, moved, brushed, wetted, arranged, stacked, backlit or removed, and no shot is composed by putting anything anywhere. The film records that the ground is covered with them; that is all it does. The red is the real colour of the real ground in real light and is never graded, gelled, sprayed, dampened or matched in from another location. No reconstruction, no re-enactment, no period dressing, no boat, no actor, nobody playing anybody's arrival. The hand and the boot in beat 4 belong to a consenting member of the crew and to nobody else: no local person, park employee, tracker or driver is asked to supply a hand, a silhouette or a walk. If anyone is encountered — staff, trackers, fishers working the coast beyond the park boundary — they are not filmed as subjects, nothing is filmed of them that they have not been asked about in a language they use, and nobody who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera appears in any frame. Wildlife is filmed at whatever distance the park's rules and the animal's own behaviour set, is never approached, baited or driven for a shot, and is not made into a character. The chronicle is attributed as a chronicle in the voice every time it is used, and the naming story is never narrated as something that happened. No drone flies unless written permission exists, and if it does not exist the film is made from the ground and from the vehicle as written.
position_hint: Middle of the group, as the change of air. It is the only film here with no architecture, no interior, no crowd and nobody in frame, so it works best set between two built sites, and it wants a viewer who has already watched a name and a thing come apart once and will therefore sit still for eight minutes of heat and an empty horizon. It also needs to be cut long and slow, which is easier to ask for once the series has a rhythm. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: The founding legend. The tradition attached to this coast is an origin story involving a woman of the island's earlier people who is used and abandoned and cursed, and it is the seed of an ethnic origin narrative this series must not go anywhere near. The film gives it one neutral clause in beat 2 and then says out loud that it is not the film's business. No community is named, characterised, filmed or made a subject, no population is described as earlier or later, and no claim about who was here first appears anywhere in the film.

Narrating the chronicle as history. The landing is tradition, not established fact, and the identification of this cape with the place the chronicle names is contested. Every beat that uses the story attributes it, and beat 3 states the absence of archaeological confirmation before the film goes any further.

Telling anybody the name they use is wrong. The C084 digest forbids it outright, and this film is about the country's own name, which makes the temptation stronger and the error worse. The argument is that a name and its basis are separate things, never that the name is a mistake; beat 8 exists to say so.

'We are all made of the same earth.' The C077 digest names this reading and refuses it: the source matches inside and outside element by element precisely to show that neither side contains a self, not to produce a feeling of belonging to a landscape. A film about red soil drifts there by default, so nothing in the voice connects the viewer's body to the ground.

Overreaching into 'nothing is real' or 'the self is an illusion'. Both digests block it. The colour, the sound and the sherds are all fully real in this system; what is not on the ground is the gathering.
Treating the existent and non-existent pairs as true and false names. They are technical Abhidhamma categories and the film never translates them into a verdict.

Drone permission. This is inside a national park where drone use is listed among the prohibited activities, and permission should be assumed refused. The film is written so that every frame in it, including the payoff, can be made from the ground or from the vehicle.

Park rules against the film's needs. The gates open at six and close at six and the point is a long way inside, so there is no dawn or dusk from this ground at all, and the late light the cliff wants collides directly with the exit time. A vehicle must not leave the track and a camera operator may not be permitted out of it in some areas.

Wild animals and the coast itself. Leopard, sloth bear and elephant are present in the park, the cliff edge is eroding actively, and the sea off the point is reported to run strong. Nothing about this film is worth a risk taken for a shot.

Disturbing or removing archaeological material, including by walking on the densest part of the scatter. The film's own subject is that the ground is covered with it, which is lost the moment anyone touches anything.

Emptiness read as an absence of film-making rather than as the film. The piece has no event, and if the long lenses, the haze and the colour are not actually got, there is nothing underneath them. This is the risk that can only be answered by the footage.
The colour not being there on the day. The ground and sand at this cape are described as varying from golden through red to black, and a dull or wet window would remove the film's entire basis.
drop_if: The cape cannot be reached and filmed within the park's permitted hours on terms the department will give, or filming is confined to what an ordinary visitor may do from a moving jeep.
The surface scatter cannot be filmed without walking on it or disturbing it.
The film cannot be made without retelling the founding legend, which is the one thing it refuses to do.
The ground does not read red on camera in any available window, or the cliff face has been cut back or slumped to the point where the two-kilometre band no longer exists as a frame.

connections.note: IDEA-0002 has taken in this record's previous film in full — the colossal brick monument, its ninety-three million units and its argument about a name laid over an assemblage. Nothing of that film survives in this record; it was repurposed to a different place, a different concept reading and a different look.

Four living names for one mountain, all in use and none of them wrong; and one dead name for a whole country, taken from the colour of the ground at one cape and now attached to nothing that cape does.
Two sites where the unsettled thing is the identification itself: figures whose names and dates nobody agrees on, and a cape that may or may not be the place a chronicle is describing.

selection.reason: It is the widest gap between a name and its basis available anywhere on the slate: the oldest recorded name for the entire country is, on the tradition's own telling, a word for the colour of the earth at one small cape, and that earth is still lying there, the same colour, doing nothing. It is also the group's only landscape with no architecture, no worship and nobody in frame, which is what the group was told it was missing.

review.note: This record has been repurposed outright. The film it used to hold — the colossal brick monument, its ninety-three million hand-sized units and its argument about a name surviving the loss of half the thing it named — has been merged into IDEA-0002 by another writer working in parallel, so that material is preserved there and nothing of it is kept here; no dome, no brick count, no terrace, no conservation masonry and no pilgrim survives anywhere in this file. The reason for the repurposing is that Chathura reviewed this group and found eight of its twelve candidates were ancient Buddhist monuments, and asked for real differentiation; this is one of three replacements written to break that monoculture, and it is deliberately the wild, unbuilt one — no monument, no temple, no worship, no architecture, no interior and nobody in frame. The new location is the cape named in suggested_location, a low cliff of red dune earth over fossil limestone on an all but empty stretch of west coast inside a national park, and the film is built on the verified record there: a chronicle tradition that the men who came ashore on that coast rested their hands on the ground, rose with palms stained the colour of copper, and gave a word meaning copper-coloured sand first to the district and then to the whole island, that word being the form attested on an emperor's rock edict three centuries before the chronicle was compiled and generally taken to be the root behind the Greek and Roman name for the island; a harbour on this coast, named by the Greeks out of their own words for horse and mountain to match a local name of the same meaning, recorded by Pliny as the landfall of the first Roman known to have reached the island, in the reign of Claudius, and a centre of the pearl trade; and a ground still covered with brickbats and an enormous quantity of potsherds, which Brohier dated no later than about fifty years before the Christian era. That gives the two concepts one site. C084 gets a name and its basis pulled as far apart as they will go — a colour word, real in itself, now designating sixty-five thousand square kilometres — and the Margaya's own third category of name, the one whose example is 'the white man', fits it exactly. C077 gets the plain sense of khandha as heap, collection and portion, standing on ground where the collection is complete and the thing collected is gone. Both concept links were re-tested against the digests from scratch and every citation was checked against the source lines rather than inherited. Guards are written into the beats, not bolted beside them: the chronicle is attributed as a chronicle and never narrated as event, the identification of the cape is recorded as contested, the founding legend's encounter with people already living there gets one neutral clause and is then explicitly set aside, no community is named or characterised and no claim about who was here first appears, the film never says anybody's name for anything is wrong, the sherds are never touched, and the digest's specific prohibition on 'we are all one with nature' is answered by keeping the viewer's body out of the voice entirely. The cliff height of 225 m repeated across travel writing is rejected: the Department of Wildlife Conservation gives an uplifted limestone cliff rising up to about 20 m and running almost 2 km from the point, and that is what the file uses, with the discrepancy recorded. Drone permission is treated as very probably refused, since drones are listed among the park's prohibited activities, and every beat including the payoff is makeable from the ground or the vehicle. Title is new; the two requested aliases are kept; a full historical_thread block replaces the old one; six Commons images were verified through the search and titles APIs and their descriptions read before the captions were written.

suggested_location.name: Kudiramalai Point

also_known_as.name: Kudiramalai / Kudrimalai / Kuthiramalai
also_known_as.meaning: horse mountain, from Tamil kudirai (horse) and malai (hill or mountain)
also_known_as.used_by: current Tamil and Sinhala usage, and the Survey Department sheets

also_known_as.name: Hipporus / Hippuros
also_known_as.meaning: read as Greek hippos (horse) and oros (mountain), a rendering of the same local meaning
also_known_as.used_by: Pliny, Natural History VI.24, and the classical geographers after him

also_known_as.name: Tambapanni / Thambapanni
also_known_as.meaning: copper-coloured sand or copper-coloured palms; Sanskrit Tāmraparṇī / Tāmravarṇī
also_known_as.used_by: the Pali chronicle tradition, which applies it to the landing district and then to the island; the identification of this cape with it is contested

suggested_location.region: Puttalam District, North Western Province — the northern end of the district, on the west coast inside Wilpattu National Park, facing the Gulf of Mannar, some 40 km north of Puttalam town and a long drive inside the park from the Hunuwilgama entrance off the A12
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place on the slate where a name and its basis are documented as far apart as they can be got, and where the basis is still physically lying there to be filmed. The chronicle tradition glosses the oldest recorded name of the entire island as a word for the colour of the earth on the hands of the men who came ashore on this coast; that earth is a two-kilometre band of deep red dune sand over pale fossil limestone with nothing built on it, nobody living at it and nothing happening on it. And twenty metres inland the same ground is covered with broken brick and an enormous quantity of potsherds from a trading town that is not there any more — a collection with nothing left to collect it, which is the plain sense of the second concept's central word. One cape, two concepts, no monument, and a payoff that is a handful of red dust rather than a reveal. It is also the group's only unbuilt, unpeopled landscape, which is the differentiation Chathura asked for.

historical_thread.story:
Kudiramalai Point is a low cape on the west coast of Sri Lanka, at the northern end of Puttalam District, inside Wilpattu National Park and facing the Gulf of Mannar. The name is Tamil and means horse mountain, from kudirai and malai. There is no monument here and no settlement at the point.

The ground is the reason the place has a history at all. The Department of Wildlife Conservation's own description of the park's geology treats Kudiramalai Point as the type section for the whole area: an uplifted limestone cliff rising up to about twenty metres above sea level and running almost two kilometres from the point, the limestone a Miocene marine formation full of fossil branching corals, molluscs and bivalves, with red layers of earth above it. The 'Red Earth' is described as a distinct reddish-brown surface formation covering roughly eighty per cent of the Wilpattu area, a very fine sand with about thirty per cent clay and silt, interpreted as marine and wind-blown in origin. A detailed facies study of the same section — Reuter and others, 'Coastal landscape evolution in the Wilpattu National Park (NW Sri Lanka) linked to changes in sediment supply and rainfall across the Pleistocene–Holocene transition', Geological Journal 55 (2020), 6642–6656, doi 10.1002/gj.3826 — identifies the red beds as red coastal dunes formed in several phases across the Pleistocene–Holocene boundary, and correlates them across the Gulf of Mannar with the Teri Sands of south-eastern India. The popular description of the cliffs as laterite is therefore loose: these are reddened dune and marine sands over limestone, not a laterite profile.

The naming story is in the Mahavamsa, the Pali chronicle compiled in the fifth or sixth century CE. In Geiger's standard English translation, as published at lakdiva.org.lk, chapter VII reads: 'When those who were commanded by Vijaya landed from their ship, they sat down wearied, resting their hands upon the ground, and since their hands were reddened by touching the dust of the red earth that region and also the island were (named) Tambapanni.' The grammar of that sentence is the whole point: a description of the colour of the ground becomes the name of a district and then of the island. Tambapanni is the Prakrit and Pali form of Sanskrit Tāmraparṇī or Tāmravarṇī, copper-coloured, and is usually glossed either as copper-coloured sand or as copper-coloured palms.

That form is attested in writing long before the chronicle that explains it. Ashoka's major rock edicts, of the third century BCE, name Tambapamni in the south alongside the Cholas and the Pandyas, which the reference literature treats as the earliest surviving written record of a name for the island. The Greek Taprobanē is generally derived from the same Prakrit or Pali form; it was reported to Europeans by Megasthenes around 290 BCE, appears in Eratosthenes, and is used by Claudius Ptolemy in the second century CE. Taprobana and its variants remained in European use into the early modern period, so a descendant of the word was still the name Europe gave the island fifteen centuries after the edicts.

The classical harbour on this coast is Hippuros. Pliny the Elder, Natural History VI.24, records that in the reign of Claudius a freedman of Annius Plocamus, who had farmed the Red Sea revenues from the treasury, was sailing round Arabia when a northerly gale carried him past the coast of Carmania, and that in the course of fifteen days he drifted to Hippuros, a port of Taprobane, where the king received him kindly; after six months he had learned enough of the language to answer the king's questions about the Romans and their emperor, and an embassy of four was sent to Rome. This is the earliest recorded direct contact between Rome and the island. Kudiramalai is commonly identified with Hippuros, and the Greek form is read as hippos, a horse, with oros, a mountain — the same meaning as the Tamil name, in entirely different sounds. The Gulf of Mannar pearl banks lie off this coast and the port is described in the local literature as a centre of the pearl trade. A separate strand of tradition attaches a legendary queen, Alli Raani, to Kudiramalai, said to have traded Mannar pearls for Arabian horses, and makes that the origin of the horse name; a large equestrian statue serving as a navigation mark is part of the same tradition. Both are legend. Wikipedia's article cites Sidebotham for a Tamil-Brahmi inscription bearing the name Korra-Puman found at Berenike in Egypt, as evidence of direct trade between this coast and the Roman east.

The archaeology is almost entirely surface archaeology. R.L. Brohier, in Discovering Ceylon (1973), reports that the buried settlement near Kudiramalai was first noticed in 1923 by H.G.A. de Silva, a Survey Department surveyor running a topographical survey of the north-western shore; Brohier went there himself and found three ancient wells and large quantities of broken brick, plates, pottery and water vessels between the surface sand and the underlying limestone, and dated the fragments to a period no later than about 50 BCE. The ground is described in the local literature as covered with brickbats and an enormous quantity of potsherds, with stratified deposits visible in the eroding cliff sections. Excavated evidence is summarised as habitation from the first century BCE to the seventh century CE. The site has been declared archaeological, but the reporting says no exploration or conservation work has been carried out by the department, that granite artefacts have been carried away by visitors, and that the sea is cutting the deposit away steadily. Inland and a little to the north-east lies Pomparippu, an urn-burial cemetery noticed by A.M. Hocart in the survey of the Puttalam–Mannar coast in 1923–24, excavated by Raja de Silva in 1956 and again in 1970 by Vimala Begley, Bennet Bronson and Mohamed Mauroof for a University of Pennsylvania project, with the urns dated by de Silva to about 200 BCE to 200 CE. This film does not go to Pomparippu, films nothing there, and takes no part in the arguments about who the people buried there were.

Access has tightened. The cape is inside the national park, which is open from six in the morning to six in the evening, requires a licensed jeep and a park tracker, and lists drone use among its prohibited activities. Reaching Kudiramalai normally means a full-day permit from the main Hunuwilgama entrance. The Eluvankulama entrance and the Eluvankulama–Mannar road, the short way in, are reported closed to the public from May 2025.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The question this history already turns on is C084's question, and it turns on it in the largest available units.

First, the name and its basis are here at maximum separation, and both ends are still available to a camera. The sources define paññatti as both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25], and a name-concept as the name laid over the ultimates or over the eight kinds of concept [C084-P:L47]. The first of those kinds is the collective, whose listed examples are the earth, mountains, rivers and the sea [C084-P:L29], and the Mārgaya's shape-concept is the ground itself, what the mind takes up from the configurations of the great elements [C084-M:L13]. On the chronicle's own telling, the basis of the oldest recorded name of this country is a colour observed on somebody's palms at one cape; the thing the name now designates is sixty-five thousand square kilometres, twenty-five districts and everybody in them. If a name were the thing it names, that sentence could not be written. The basis has not moved, not changed colour, and has nothing whatever to do with anything the word now does — and it is lying in the frame.

Second, the sixfold scheme of names has this exact case in it, which is why the site is right and not merely apt. The Mārgaya's example of the third kind, a name resting on something ultimately real and designating something not ultimately real, is 'the white man': white is a real state, it is colour-form; the man is not ultimately existent [C084-M:L29]. Copper-coloured sand is that structure with a country on the far end of it. The colour is real in this system and the film says so out loud; the designation is a conventional whole. And the Pradeepika forecloses any triumph in that observation by listing ground and mountain among the not-ultimately-existent and then recording, in the next breath and without embarrassment, that people call them ground and mountain [C084-P:L55]. The film's finding is that a name and its basis are two items. It is not that anybody is wrong, and the digest's bar on telling a participant their name is wrong governs the beat that closes the film.

Third, the record shows the sound and the meaning coming apart in the most literal way this concept could ask for. The Mārgaya keeps the spoken sound ultimately real and the name it carries a concept, arising in whoever is listening [C084-M:L21]. Here the sounds physically travelled and were reshaped at every hearing: the Prakrit form cut into an emperor's rock three centuries before the chronicle that explains it, a Greek spelling, a Roman copy, and a European descendant still in use fifteen hundred years later. And the traffic ran the other way too. The Greeks took a local name meaning horse mountain and built their own name for the harbour out of their own words for horse and mountain: the meaning arrived intact and not one of the sounds did. That is the sound-versus-name distinction as documentary fact rather than as an example.

Fourth, C077 stops the film from becoming a piece about etymology, and it does so on the same ground twenty metres further inland. Khandha is the ordinary word for a heap: the Pradeepika sorts its several senses and keeps only that one, the sense used of a great heap of water, expressly setting aside the conventional sense used of a great log of firewood, and says the aggregates are characterised by heap-ness and by being portions [C077-P:L36–L42]; it shows the whole mass of one kind lumped together on all sides under one word [C077-P:L44], and makes one heap by gathering into one place the parts alike in a single characteristic [C077-P:L996–L998]; the Mārgaya says the word means collection [C077-M:L10]. A town that traded across an ocean is now a surface of sherds: every portion present, the whole absent, and nothing on the site doing the gathering. The eleven aspects across which a heap reaches — past, future, present, internal, external, coarse, fine, inferior, superior, far, near [C077-P:L46–L57] — are why that is not a trick of language: the collection is expressly allowed to include what is over. The film can therefore point at the ground and say the collecting is happening in a mind, without saying that the sherds are unreal or that nobody is standing there.

What the history cannot be used for is the thing it is most often used for. The landing is chronicle, not archaeology; the dated material on this cape is five centuries later than the tradition's date; and the identification of this cape as the chronicle's landing place is contested. The film therefore uses the naming story as a story about a name, which is the only part of it that is documented — the chronicle's own sentence — and refuses the rest. The founding legend's encounter with people already living here gets one neutral clause and is then set aside on camera, no population is described as earlier or later, no community is named, and nothing in this film adjudicates anything about who anybody is descended from. That refusal is not a compromise forced on the film; the concept does not need the legend, and the colour of the ground is a better witness than any of it.
what_is_certain: Kudiramalai Point is a cape on the west coast of Sri Lanka, at the northern end of Puttalam District, inside Wilpattu National Park, facing the Gulf of Mannar. Wikipedia and Wikidata give its position as 8°32′0″N 79°52′0″E.
The name is Tamil and means horse mountain, from kudirai (horse) and malai (hill or mountain).

The Department of Wildlife Conservation's account of Wilpattu's geology describes Kudiramalai Point as a typical site for a cross section of the area, with an uplifted limestone cliff rising up to about 20 m above sea level and running almost 2 km from the point; the limestone is a Miocene marine formation containing fossils of branching corals, molluscs and bivalves, and carries red layers of earth above it.

The same account describes the park's 'Red Earth' as a distinct reddish-brown surface soil formation covering about 80 per cent of the Wilpattu area, a very fine sand with approximately 30 per cent clay and silt, interpreted as originating from marine and aeolian processes.

Reuter and others, 'Coastal landscape evolution in the Wilpattu National Park (NW Sri Lanka) linked to changes in sediment supply and rainfall across the Pleistocene–Holocene transition', Geological Journal 55 (2020) 6642–6656, doi 10.1002/gj.3826, analyses the lithological section at the Point Kudiramalai sea cliff, identifies the Red Beds as red coastal dunes formed in a multi-phase process across the Pleistocene–Holocene boundary, and correlates the section with the Teri Sands of south-eastern India across the Gulf of Mannar.

The Mahavamsa, compiled in the fifth or sixth century CE, gives the naming of Tambapanni in chapter VII. Geiger's standard English translation, as published at lakdiva.org.lk, reads: 'When those who were commanded by Vijaya landed from their ship, they sat down wearied, resting their hands upon the ground, and since their hands were reddened by touching the dust of the red earth that region and also the island were (named) Tambapanni.' The chronicle applies the name first to the region and then to the island.

Tambapanni is the Prakrit and Pali form of Sanskrit Tāmraparṇī or Tāmravarṇī, meaning copper-coloured; it is glossed in the reference literature both as copper-coloured sand and as copper-coloured palms.

Ashoka's major rock edicts of the third century BCE name Tambapamni in the south alongside the Cholas and the Pandyas. The reference literature treats these edicts as the earliest surviving written records giving a name for the island.

The Greek Taprobanē is generally derived from the Prakrit or Pali Tambapanni; it was reported to Europeans by Megasthenes around 290 BCE, appears in Eratosthenes, and is used by Claudius Ptolemy in the second century CE. Taprobana and its variants remained in European usage into the early modern period.

Pliny the Elder, Natural History VI.24, records that in the reign of Claudius a freedman of Annius Plocamus, who had farmed the Red Sea revenues from the treasury, was carried by a northerly gale past the coast of Carmania while sailing round Arabia, drifted in the course of fifteen days to Hippuros, a port of Taprobane, was hospitably received by the king, learned the language in six months, answered the king's questions about the Romans and their emperor, and that an embassy of four was subsequently sent to Rome.
The Greek form Hipporus or Hippuros is read in the local literature as compounded from hippos, a horse, and oros, a mountain, matching the meaning of the Tamil name.

R.L. Brohier, Discovering Ceylon (1973), records that the buried settlement near Kudiramalai was first noticed in 1923 by H.G.A. de Silva, a Survey Department surveyor conducting a topographical survey off the island's north-western shore; that Brohier visited and found three ancient wells together with large quantities of broken bricks, plates, pottery and water-collecting vessels between the surface sand and the underlying limestone; and that the fragments belong to a period no later than about 50 BCE.

The ground at the site is described in the local literature as covered with brickbats and an enormous quantity of pottery fragments, with stratified remains visible in the eroded coastal cliff sections. Wikipedia summarises the excavated evidence as indicating habitation from the first century BCE to the seventh century CE.

The reporting states that although the site is declared archaeological, no exploration or conservation work has been carried out by the department, that granite artefacts scattered on the site have been carried away, and that coastal erosion is actively destroying the deposit and has already washed away much of the visible ruin.

Pomparippu, inland of the cape, is an urn-burial cemetery. It was noticed by A.M. Hocart during the survey of the Puttalam–Mannar coast in 1923–24, urn burials were excavated by Raja de Silva in 1956, and further excavation was carried out in July and August 1970 by Vimala Begley, Bennet Bronson and Mohamed Mauroof for a University of Pennsylvania project. De Silva dated the urn burials to about 200 BCE to 200 CE; the urns are reported as 40–90 cm in diameter, placed in pits and sealed with limestone boulders, with skulls often set in dishes of Black-and-Red Ware.

Wilpattu National Park is open from 6.00 to 18.00; safaris outside those hours are not permitted; self-driving is not allowed and visits are made in licensed 4×4 jeeps with a guide or tracker; the main entrance is at Hunuwilgama, off the A12 between Puttalam and Anuradhapura; drone use is listed among the prohibited activities, along with pets, smoking, alcohol, littering and touching animals or plants.

The Eluvankulama entrance and the Eluvankulama–Mannar road have been reported closed to the public since May 2025; an entrance ticket from the park office at the Eluvankulama low-water crossing was previously required to turn off that road onto the jungle track to Kudiramalai.
Leopard, sloth bear and elephant are present in Wilpattu. Travel guidance commonly gives February to October as the best window, the heaviest rain falling roughly October to December.
what_is_disputed: The landing of Vijaya is chronicle tradition and not established fact. There is no archaeological evidence for the narrative as the Mahavamsa gives it — no inscription, coin or material assemblage tied to a king of that name or to the founding of a kingdom called Tambapanni in the sixth century BCE — and the chronicle was compiled some nine or ten centuries after the events it describes. The film attributes the story to a chronicle every time it uses it and never narrates it as something that happened.

The identification of this cape as the place the chronicle means is contested. The Mahavamsa's landing district is variously located near Mannar, at Chilaw, at this cape and elsewhere; Keerimalai on the northern coast is also proposed on the same grounds, that copper-coloured soil is found there close to the shore; and at least one study consulted rejects the generally accepted Mannar-area reading outright. The local literature's own formulation is that the landing is 'firmly believed' to have been between Kudiramalai Point and the mouth of the Moderagam Aru, which is a statement of belief and is recorded here as one.

That Tambapanni is the oldest name of the island rests on the Ashokan edicts being the earliest surviving written record of a name for it, which is what the reference literature consulted states. The earliest attestations of Sīhala, Lankā and the other traditional names were not established in this research, and nothing here should be read as putting the island's names in an order of age.

The derivation of Greek Taprobanē from Tambapanni is described in the reference literature as a theory and as 'suggested', not as settled. One alternative is a derivation from the Tamraparni river of southern India rather than from the island's own name.

The cliff height. Several travel and heritage sites, following one another, state that 'Kudiramalai Cape is a high cliff about 225 m tall consisting of two strata of tertiary sandstone in the upper layer'. That figure is not credible for this cape and is contradicted by the Department of Wildlife Conservation's own geological description, which gives an uplifted limestone cliff rising up to about 20 m above sea level. This file uses about 20 m and records the 225 m figure as an error propagated through secondary writing.

The description of the cliffs and soil as laterite is popular usage. The geological literature treats them as reddened coastal dune and marine sands over Miocene limestone, correlated with the Teri Sands of south-eastern India, which is not a laterite profile. The film describes the colour, which is not in doubt, and not a rock type.

Who noticed what in 1923. Brohier credits H.G.A. de Silva, a Survey Department surveyor, with first noticing the buried habitation near Kudiramalai; the literature on the urn burials credits A.M. Hocart with noticing Pomparippu during the 1923–24 survey of the same coast. These may be two findings from one survey season, or the two credits may have been run together in secondary writing. Nothing is inferred from it.

Brohier's date of 'no later than about 50 BCE' for the pottery reaches this research through secondary quotation of Discovering Ceylon, not through a stratigraphic report, and is not a radiometric date. Wikipedia's summary of the occupation as first century BCE to seventh century CE is likewise a summary; the excavation reports behind it were not read.

The identification of Pliny's Hippuros with this cape is a reasonable and widely repeated reading resting largely on the horse-and-mountain etymology; no inscription or excavated find ties Pliny's port to this point. The Greek etymology itself is given in the local literature and was not checked against a lexicon.

Alli Raani, the legendary queen said to have ruled this coast from Kudiramalai and to have traded Mannar pearls for Arabian horses, and the tradition of a large equestrian statue used as a navigation mark, are legend. The palace ruins usually attached to her name are at a separate site on the Puttalam peninsula, not at this cape, and the two are frequently conflated. The film uses none of it as fact.

The Tamil-Brahmi inscription naming Korra-Puman, found at Berenike and cited as evidence of direct trade with this coast, reaches this research through Wikipedia's citation of Sidebotham and was not checked against the publication.

Above all: nothing in this record is evidence about who lived on this coast first, or about the ancestry of anybody living now. The chronicle tradition, the urn burials at Pomparippu and the trading record are three separate bodies of material of three different kinds, and the arguments that have been built on them about population origins are not entered here, are not adjudicated, and do not appear in the film in any form.

what_to_film: The long-lens compression down the coast from the point: the red band, the pale limestone band and the sea reduced to three flat planes with heat visibly moving between them. This is the film's establishing idea and it needs the longest glass available and a very still tripod.

The cliff face itself in late light from beach level, close enough to read the courses: red dune earth sitting on grey-white limestone, fossil coral in the rock, dry red run-off streaking the pale stone.

The emptiness, honestly and at length: a horizon with nothing on it, held long enough to become the subject; the scrub line moving in the sea wind with nothing else moving; a jeep track filling in behind the vehicle.

The red ground very close and very small — dust on skin, a crumb broken between finger and thumb, the colour under the edge of a boot. This is the payoff frame, it is intimate rather than grand, and it must be lit by nothing but the day.

The surface of potsherds and broken brick, from above and from knee height, wide enough to read as a continuous texture and close enough to read as individual rims and bases. Filmed with a long lens from a standing position and from the vehicle wherever possible, so that the densest part of the scatter is never walked on and nothing is touched.
The eroding edge where the deposit meets the sea: sand, sherd layer and limestone in section, with the sea working at the bottom of it.

The drive in, as the film's only movement: sand track, thorn scrub, the villus and dry pans of the park, the vegetation dropping in height as the wind off the sea increases, and then the ground going red.

Whatever the day gives at distance and never approached: birds over the shallows, deer or buffalo crossing far off, a track in the dust. None of it is a character and none of it is worth a second attempt.
suggested_location.access: Inside Wilpattu National Park, so entirely on the park's terms. Open 06.00 to 18.00 only; no self-driving; entry in a licensed 4×4 with a park tracker or guide, ticketed at the main Hunuwilgama entrance off the A12 between Puttalam and Anuradhapura. Kudiramalai Point is a long run inside the park on sand tracks and normally needs a full-day permit — operators quote around a hundred kilometres of driving for a full-day circuit. The short way in from the south, the Eluvankulama entrance and the Eluvankulama–Mannar road, is reported closed to the public from May 2025; before that, turning onto the jungle track to the cape required an entrance ticket from the park office at the Eluvankulama low-water crossing. Drone use is listed among the park's prohibited activities and should be assumed refused; any flight would need Civil Aviation Authority registration and permit as well as the department's written consent, and the film is written so that it does not depend on one. Filming beyond ordinary visitor terms — a tripod outside the vehicle, time at one spot, a second day — needs Department of Wildlife Conservation permission that has not been sought. The archaeological surface is separately protected and nothing on it may be handled. Puttalam town is about forty kilometres south and is the practical base; Colombo to Puttalam is roughly 150–170 km and three to four hours.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry, bright half of the year. General guidance for the park is February to October, with the heaviest rain roughly October to December, and this coast is at its most saturated in colour in clear hard weather rather than soft weather. Within the day, the cape faces west into open sea, so the red face takes direct light in the last two hours before the park closes at six — which is also the exit deadline, so the best light and the end of the permitted day arrive together and the schedule has to be built backwards from it. There is no true sunrise or sunset available from this ground at all, since the gates open at six and shut at six and the point is hours inside; the film is made in hard daylight and late afternoon. Midday, which is useless almost everywhere else, is when the heat haze is thickest and is the right time for the long-lens compression shots.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 25 September 2026, none of it checked on the ground or against printed editions. Coordinates are Wikipedia's and Wikidata's, and match the GPS tags on the Commons photographs of the cape; they were not verified against a survey sheet. The cliff height was the one figure that had to be resolved. A cluster of travel and heritage pages repeat, word for word, that the cape is 'a high cliff about 225 m tall consisting of two strata of tertiary sandstone'; that figure is not credible for this coast and is contradicted by the Department of Wildlife Conservation's own geology page, which gives an uplifted limestone cliff rising up to about 20 m above sea level and running almost 2 km from the point. This file uses about 20 m and records the 225 m claim as propagated error. The DWC page itself returned 404 on direct fetch and its wording reached this research through search indexing, which is a weakness; the Reuter and others 2020 paper in Geological Journal is the stronger source for the same section and its abstract was read, but the full text is paywalled and only the abstract and the search-indexed description were available. The Mahavamsa wording is Geiger's translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk, chapter VII, printed there without verse numbers. Pliny VI.24 was read in the Bostock and Riley translation as reproduced online and not in a critical edition. Brohier's date for the pottery, the 'brickbats and enormous quantity of potsherds' description, the pearl trade and the Alli Raani material all come from Sri Lankan secondary writing — AmazingLanka, LankaPradeepa, the Sunday Times — and were cross-read between at least two of them; Discovering Ceylon itself was not read. The Daily Mirror article on the buried city returned 403 and was not read. Access, hours, the drone prohibition and the closure of the Eluvankulama road come from the park's visitor guidance and from travel and news reporting, and none of it has been confirmed with the Department of Wildlife Conservation; permitted filming beyond ordinary visitor terms is unverified. The Pomparippu material is included in the historical thread only to record what is nearby; the film does not go there and the population-origin arguments attached to that site are deliberately not entered. Six Wikimedia Commons files were found through the search API with a descriptive user agent, confirmed to exist through action=query&titles=, and their uploader descriptions, licences and GPS tags read before the captions were written; five are of the cape itself and the sixth is explicitly captioned as the park's soil photographed elsewhere. One uploader's own note — that the sand colour here varies from golden to red to black — is the most useful single piece of information found in this research and is carried into the risks and drop_if.

unknowns: No access, permission or contact has been sought or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.

Whether the Department of Wildlife Conservation will permit filming at the cape beyond ordinary visitor terms — a tripod outside the vehicle, extended time at one place, more than one day, a return in the last hour of light — is unverified, and the film needs at least some of it.

Drone permission is very probably refused. Drone use is listed among the park's prohibited activities, and a flight would need Civil Aviation Authority registration and permit as well as the department's written consent. The film is built so that nothing in it, including the payoff, depends on a drone; the establishing frames are long-lens from the ground and the movement comes from the vehicle.
Whether the Department of Archaeology has any standing conditions for filming a declared but unexcavated and unconserved surface site, and whom permission would come from, is unknown.

The present state of the ground is unknown. The reporting says erosion is actively cutting the deposit away and that material has been removed by visitors, so how dense the surface scatter still is, and how much of the cliff section survives, can only be established on site.
Whether the red reads red in the available window. The colour is reported to vary at this cape from golden through red to black, and no source consulted explains what governs it.
The cliff height of about 20 m rests on a single official description that could not be fetched directly, and no contour or survey figure was obtained.
Whether the point can be reached and worked and left inside the 06.00–18.00 window with enough time at the cape to make this film, given the length of the drive, has not been tested.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's, awaiting Chathura's verdict; all of its supporting detail is desk research from published secondary sources and is unverified, the chronicle material is tradition rather than established fact and is labelled as such throughout, and every measurement in it is a figure taken from a source rather than made. No scene or shot is decided here.
